summary: For learners aged 10–11, build the skill of justifying a biological classification with evidence: not just placing an organism in a group, but giving at least two specific, observable, diagnostic characteristics as reasons, and distinguishing those from features that two similar organisms share. The core move is separating characteristics that are decisive for the comparison being made (e.g. has a backbone, for vertebrate vs invertebrate; makes its own food, for green plants vs animals; breathes air with lungs rather than gills, for dolphin vs shark, though not unique to mammals; feeds young on milk, for mammals) from irrelevant or merely shared ones (colour, size, where it lives, 'swims'). This turns classification into a claim backed by evidence — an instance of argument from evidence. Activities span constructing and defending a justification, a worked-example comparison of look-alikes, and selected-response checks of what counts as decisive evidence.
misconceptions: Justifying with shared features that don't distinguish (a dolphin is a fish 'because it has fins and lives in the sea') — citing non-diagnostic evidence.
Treating classification as a guess or assertion rather than a claim that needs evidence.
Using irrelevant characteristics (colour, size, name) as if they were classifying features.
Giving only one reason, or restating the group name, instead of citing specific distinguishing characteristics.

activities.title: Classification detective: prove the placement
steps: Examine an unfamiliar organism (photo or description — e.g. a pangolin or an axolotl) and collect the features it actually shows. A pangolin is covered in scales, but it has some hair on its face and underside, and the description says it feeds its young on milk, so it is a mammal. An axolotl has a backbone and external gills, but fish share both. Its four legs with toes and its moist, scaleless skin are the features that point to amphibian.
Decide which group it belongs to and file it there.
Pin at least TWO features that justify the decision — reasons, not just a placement.
Then meet a decoy pair: a dolphin beside a shark. First try to justify using 'lives in the sea, streamlined, has fins'; notice these features are shared by BOTH animals so they decide nothing.

Search for the features that actually separate them — the dolphin breathes air with lungs through a blowhole while the shark uses gills, and the dolphin feeds its young on milk while the shark does not — and use those to settle that the dolphin is a mammal and the shark is a fish.
State the full argument: claim (it's a mammal), evidence (feeds young on milk, breathes air), reasoning (only mammals do both).
activities.insight: A scientific classification is an argument built on distinguishing evidence, not a guess from surface looks; features two look-alikes share cannot decide between them.

activities.title: Defend it: taxonomist challenge dialogue
steps: State a classification of an organism and your supporting evidence aloud or in writing.
Respond to a taxonomist who probes each justification: 'You say mammal — what's your evidence? The shark also has fins, so why isn't the dolphin a fish?'
Drop any reason the challenger shows is shared or irrelevant, and replace it with a decisive, distinguishing characteristic.
Keep going until you can name a feature present in your claimed group and absent in the look-alike group, and explain why it settles the case.
activities.insight: A classification must survive challenge: defensible reasons cite characteristics that separate the claimed group from the alternative being compared, and you can discard a reason once you see a similar organism shares it.

activities.title: Worked-example read: shared vs diagnostic features
steps: Study an annotated comparison of two look-alikes (e.g. dolphin vs shark), where features the two share are marked one way and the features that distinguish them (e.g. lungs vs gills, feeding young on milk) are marked another.
Name, for that pair, which observed features are shared and which features separate the groups.
Explain in your own words why the shared features cannot decide the classification.
activities.insight: Before constructing an argument, learners can see explicitly that some observed features are shared (non-deciding) while others are diagnostic.

activities.title: Check: which evidence is decisive?
steps: For a classified organism, select the TWO characteristics that best justify the classification (multi-select).
Match organism pairs to a feature that distinguishes their groups.
Judge whether a given reason is decisive or merely shared/irrelevant (e.g. is 'lives in the sea' good evidence that something is a fish?).
Critique a wrong justification built on a shared or irrelevant feature and say what makes it weak.
activities.insight: Recognising which evidence is diagnostic reinforces the standard for a good classification argument; recognising a reason is not the same as independently constructing and defending one.

checkQuestion: Give the child a photo of an unfamiliar animal (e.g. a pangolin or an axolotl) and one or two look-alikes. Set the task and watch: 'Decide which group this animal belongs to, and convince me using only what you can actually see — give me at least two features as your evidence. Then compare it with this similar-looking animal and tell me the one feature that settles which group each is in.' Do not supply features yourself.
checkAnswer: Selects diagnostic, observable characteristics (e.g. fur + gives live young → mammal; moist skin + gills → amphibian) and cites at least two as evidence for the decision. When comparing look-alikes, isolates the feature that truly distinguishes the groups (scales vs fur, gills vs lungs) rather than a shared superficial one (both swim).
